A Brief Survey of the Mahāpurāṇas
A brief survey of the contents of these eighteen पुराणस्, traditionally called the Mahāpurāṇas, may now be taken up here.
AGNIPURĀṆA
Agni, the god of fire, is said to have communicated this purāṇa to the sage वसिष्ठ. Though it is essentially a śaivite work, a large part of it has been devoted to the cult of विष्णु also, especially to the description of his incarnations as राम and कृष्ण.
The contents of this purāṇa are of an encyclopaedic character. Some of the subjects dealt with are: the ten incarnations of विष्णु, the stories of Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, rules regarding the worship of various deities, installation of images in temples, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, architecture and sculpture, the science of medicine, toxicology, principles of dramaturgy, human physiology, figures of speech and so on.
BHĀGAVATAPURĀṆA
By far, the most well-known of all the पुराणस्, the Bhāgavata, also called Srīmad Bhāgavata, is considered as the most authoritative text dealing with श्रीकृष्ण’s life and doings. The book, however, deals extensively with the stories of other incarnations of विष्णु also. The work is in the form of a narration by the young sage शुक (son of व्यास) to the king परीक्षित्, at his request to listen to the glories of Lord कृष्ण-वासुदेव. This purāṇa deals with the following topics: story of the king परीक्षित् and the beginning of the narration of the Bhāgavata; the cosmic form of God and च्रेअतिओन् of the world; curse incurred by जय and विजय, the attendants of Lord विष्णु as also the story of हिरण्यकशिपु and the child-devotee प्रह्लाद; story of the great sage कपिल; story of the destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice by रुद्र; story of another child-devotee ध्रुव; story of जडभरत; the descent of the river गङ्गा to the earth; the destruction of त्रिपुर or the three cities by शिव; the story of the churning of the ocean and of वामन.
The tenth book contains the story of श्रीकृष्ण in detail. The eleventh book contains the famous Uddhavagītā. The work ends with a long list of the kings that ruled after कृष्ण’s ascension and a graphic description of कलियुग, the age in which we are now living.
The Bhāgavata has many Sanskrit commentaries which are very useful in understanding it.
BHAVIṢYAPURĀṆA
The printed texts of this purāṇa comprise two parts: Pūrvārdha and Utta-rārdha. However, many scholars consider the latter half as an independent treatise and call it as Bhaviṣyottarapurāṇa.
The Bhaviṣyapurāṇa is a veritable storehouse of several topics normally dealt with in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. The following is the list of some selected topics: the sixteen सṁस्कारस् or sacraments like नामकरण and उपनयन; rules concerning the study of the वेदस्; some aspects of varṇāśrama-धर्म; a good number of vratas or religious observances slated for certain days; snakes and their worship; praise and worship of सूर्य, the sun-god; च्रेअतिओन् of this world and a description of this earth; several types of दान or giving gifts ceremonially; description of good conduct.
A very interesting aspect of this purāṇa is the bringing of the Maga ब्राह्मणस् from the Śākadvīpa into our country by Sāmba, son of श्रीकृष्ण and getting them settled on the banks of the river चन्द्रभागा. They were Zoroastrians from Persia. They gradually integrated themselves into the Hindu society. Sun-worship in India got a boost because of them.
This purāṇa has been called Bhaviṣyapurāṇa, purāṇa predicting future events, probably because it gives the genealogy of the kings who will come in future and the way they rule the country.
BRAHMAPURĀṆA
The Brahmapurāṇa that is now available in print, seems to be more a compilation of chapters taken from some other works like the Mahābhārata, विष्णुपुराण, Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa and Vāyupurāṇa, though it does contain original material also, dealing chiefly with the praise of the shrines and holy places in the पुरुषोत्तम-क्षेत्र (Puri in Orissa), Koṇarka (Konārak), एकाम्र-क्षेत्र (Bhubaneswar) and others.
Its contents may be summarised as follows: च्रेअतिओन् of the world including the gods and human beings; geographical details of this world as comprising the seven dvīpas or island-continents; the story of दक्ष’s sacrifice; descriptions of some well-known places of पिल्ग्रिमगे; detailed treatment of the पुरुषोत्तम-क्षेत्र, including the temple of Jagannātha and its images; descent of the river गङ्गा; descriptions of several other holy places; story of श्रीकृष्ण in detail; descriptions of some avatāras of विष्णु like Varāha and नरसिṁह; the paths of Sāṅkhya and योग.
BRAHMĀṆḌAPURĀṆA
The Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa is divided into four pādas or parts: Prakriyāpāda, Anuṣaṅgapāda, Upodghātapāda and Upasaṁhārapāda. This is followed by Lalitopākhyāna in 40 chapters.
It is said to have been taught by ब्रह्मा himself to the sages engaged in a सत्त्रयाग in the Naimiṣa forest. The first two parts deal with the subjects of च्रेअतिओन् (from the ब्रह्माण्ड or the cosmic egg), the geography of the earth and of भारतवर्ष, the manvantaras, pupils of व्यास and the distribution of the Vedic शाखास्. The third section deals with all aspects of śrāddha (after-death rites), of परशुराम’s exploits, descent of गङ्गा by the efforts of भगीरथ, the story of धन्वन्तरि receiving the आयुर्वेद (the science of health and longevity) and so on.
The fourth section deals with the future मनुस्, the कल्प-प्रलय (final dissolution at the end of a cycle), a description of the fourteen worlds as also the various types of hells. There is also a beautiful philosophical disquisition of ब्रह्मन् or परमात्मन् (God) who is beyond all लोगिच् and reasoning.
Lalitopākhyāna contains the famous Lalitāsahasranāma, a hymn endowed with mystical powers.
Sometimes, the well-known Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa is stated to be a part of this Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
Hundreds of verses of this purāṇa are found in the Vāyupurāṇa also. Hence scholars sometimes surmise that the two पुराणस् were originally one—called Vāyavīya-ब्रह्माण्ड-purāṇa—and might have got separated around A. D. 400.
A Balineese translation of this purāṇa has been found in the बलि island of Indonesia.
BRAHMAVAIVARTAPURĀṆA
The original Brahmavaivartapurāṇa might have been a more ancient work—earlier than A. D. 300—since the Viṣṇupurāṇa has mentioned it among the Mahāpurāṇas. The text now available in print may have been evolved during the period A. D. 800-1600.
Since the original cause of the universe has been depicted here as a ‘vivarta’ or ‘appearance’ of ब्रह्मन्, this purāṇa has been designated as Brahmavaivartapurāṇa.
The Brahmakhaṇḍa, the first section, traces the evolution of the universe from the four-faced ब्रह्मा who is also श्रीकृष्ण himself. The Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, the second, describes the emanations of दुर्गा, लक्ष्मी, सरस्वती, सावित्री and राधा from the Mūlaprakṛti, as per the command of श्रीकृष्ण. The Gaṇeśakhaṇḍa describes in detail, the birth and exploits of गणेश and षण्मुख, the two sons of शिव and पार्वती. The last section, the Śrīkṛṣṇa-janmakhaṇḍa deals with the story of श्रीकृष्ण and his divine consort राधा. This section is almost as big as the other three sections put together.
A good number of interesting topics have been dealt with in this purāṇa. To mention only a few: आयुर्वेद or the science of health and longevity; the सन्ध्या ritual; importance of शालग्राम and its worship; description of the कलियुग (Iron Age); the merits of taking bath in the गङ्गा river on auspicious days; greatness of the तुलसी leaves (holy basil); story of सावित्री and सत्यवान्; story of Manasādevī, the goddess of snakes; दुर्गापूजा; prognostication through द्रेअम्स्; code of conduct for married women and widows; greatness of Bhāratadeśa or India; some instructions regarding building construction.
GARUḌAPURĀṆA
Though some scholars feel that this is a spurious Vaiṣṇava work, probably composed in the tenth century, it is held in high esteem even now. Its recitation, especially during the performance of the death and after-death ceremonies is consi-dered auspicious, since it deals with the topic of एस्छतोलोग्य् in great detail.
The number of verses attributed to this purāṇa seems to vary from about 8000 to 19,000.
The name Garuḍapurāṇa has been derived from the fact that it was taught by Lord विष्णु to his eagle-mount गरुड.
The first part of this work, like the Agnipurāṇa, is encyclopaedic in character, dealing with several topics such as the contents of the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, cosmography, अस्त्रोनोम्य्, अस्त्रोलोग्य्, omens and portents, medicine and knowledge of precious stones.
The second part, called Pretakalpa deals in great detail with death, the journey of the जीव after death to its next destination, the various rites to be performed at death and after death, torments of हेल्ल्, encounter with pretas or spirits of the dead, the यमलोक or the world of यम (the god of death and हेल्ल्) and लिबेरतिओन् through devotion to Lord विष्णु.
KŪRMAPURĀṆA
The present Kūrmapurāṇa comprising two parts claims to be the first section—called Brāhmīsaṁhitā—of a much bigger work consisting of four saṁhitās or sections viz., Brāhmī, Bhāgavatī, Saurī and Vaiṣṇavī. However the last three seem to have been lost.
This purāṇa was, perhaps, a pāñca-rātra work which was later recast by the pāśupatas during the eighth century A. D.
Lord विष्णु taught this purāṇa in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as कूर्म or tortoise, to the sages like नारद. Hence the name Kūrmapurāṇa.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be presented here: the duties of the four varṇas and the four āśramas; evolution of the प्रकृति (primeval nature) into the world; story of Svāyambhuva मनु and his wife Śatarūpā; story of दक्ष; story of वामन and बलि; genealogies of some ṛṣis and kings; description of the yaduvaṁśa (the lineage of the king यदु); greatness of काशी and प्रयाग, the two well-known pilgrim centres; description of the physical features of the world and of जम्बूद्वीप which contains भारतवर्ष; division of the वेदस्; the famous Īśvaragītā; on śrāddhas or after-death rites; on prāyaścittas or expiations for sins; प्रलय or destruction of the created world.
LIṄGAPURĀṆA
This purāṇa mainly aims at the propagation of the cult of शिव and his worship through the लिङ्ग, the rounded surface emblem commonly worshipped even now.
It deals with a number of subjects, the more important ones being: the manifestation of the five aspects of शिव viz., सद्योजात, वामदेव, Tatpuruṣa, अघोर and ईशान; शिव appearing as a huge pillar of fire to ब्रह्मा and विष्णु; व्यास and his disciples; stories of the sages दधीचि and Śilāda; about the four युगस् or epochs; नन्दि and his worship; descriptions of the well-known Sūryavaṁśa and चन्द्र-vaṁśa, the dynasties originating from the sun and the मोओन्; worship of शिव and description of some vratas; detailed account of the famous Śivapañcākṣarī-मन्त्र and its use in meditation; an account of the places of पिल्ग्रिमगे like काशी; on मुसिच् and its propagation; manifestation of शिव in eight forms (aṣṭa-mūrtis); various dānas or gifts and their fruits; how to establish the Śivaliṅgas; the mṛtyuñjaya-मन्त्र and its usage.
Several subsidiary religious works like Pañcākṣara-māhātmya, Rāmasahasra-nāma and Rudrākṣa-māhātmya have originated from this purāṇa.
MĀRKAṆḌEYAPURĀṆA
This is one of the few पुराणस् that have retained much of the more ancient material, composed probably around A. D. 300.
Though this work is said to contain 9000 verses, the printed texts available now fall short of it by nearly 2000 verses.
The purāṇa starts with the questions posed by जैमिनि to the sage मार्कण्डेय who directs him to the four caṭaka birds living in the Vindhyācala range of hills. The birds later on refer to the teachings of मार्कण्डेय given to Krauṣṭuki. The well-known and extremely popular work, the Devīmāhātmya (also called Caṇḍī and Durgāsaptaśatī), forms an integral part of this purāṇa.
The Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa is remarkably non-sectarian in character. The Vedic deities, इन्द्र, ब्रह्मा, अग्नि and सूर्य, as also the sun-myths, get greater coverage than विष्णु or शिव. There is a clear trend towards popularising the śrauta and the smārta rites which had already begun to be neglected by the people.
Apart from the usual subjects of च्रेअतिओन्, dissolution, the manvantaras and genealogies, this purāṇa has also dealt with the following topics: legends of हरिश्चन्द्र, Kārtavīrya and also of the queen मदालसा; descriptions of हेल्ल्, कर्म and its fructification; some aspects of योग; geographical description of Bhārata and śrāddhas.
MATSYAPURĀṆA
Said to have been taught by Lord विष्णु in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as Matsya (or fish), this purāṇa though containing ancient material, seems to be a conglome-ration of chapters taken from various sources, especially the Vāyu and the Viṣṇudharmottara purāṇas. Some scholars feel that it was originally a Vaiṣṇava work, later on modified by the Śaivas.
In addition to dealing with the usual topics of the ancient पुराणस् like च्रेअतिओन्, dissolution and genealogies of ṛṣis and kings, this purāṇa contributes substantially to the other areas of knowledge also. Some of the topics delineated are: the stories of कच, Devayānī, ययाति and Puru; genealogies of the ब्राह्मणस् who were worshippers of fire; various vratas or religious vows; some dānas or gifts and their fruits; greatness of the holy places प्रयाग, वाराणसी and the river नर्मदा; duties of a king; on omens; some aspects of इचोनोग्रफ्य्; building construction and so on.
A remarkable feature of this purāṇa is that the last chapter (ch. 290) beautifully summarises all the subjects dealt within it, without omitting any.
NĀRADĪYAPURĀṆA
The utility of this purāṇa lies in the fact that it gives the synopsis of all the other पुराणस् also.
It is in two parts. The first part incorporates the entire work, known as Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa. The second part appears more like an independent treatise.
It comprises the teachings given to नारद by सनक and others. The subjects touched upon are of a very wide range. They include: the vratas or religious observances of the whole year; devotion to विष्णु; च्रेअतिओन् of the world; duties of the people of various varṇas and āśramas; the six वेदाङ्गस् like व्याकरण (grammar), छन्दस् (prosody) and jyotiṣa (astronomy); greatness of प्रयाग, the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे; ritualistic worship; greatness and importance of ड़स्तिन्ग् on एकादशी days and so on.
Another remarkable feature of this purāṇa is that it deals with a number of mantras and the methods of repeating them, which is a speciality of the तन्त्रस् and the आगमस्.
There is one Lalitāsahasranāma given in the 89th chapter of the first half. This, however, is entirely different from the one that is now commonly chanted, which is a part of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
PADMAPURĀṆA
This is a voluminous work in five parts: Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, Bhūmikhaṇḍa, Svargakhaṇḍa, Pātālakhaṇḍa and Uttara-khaṇḍa.
Primarily a scripture of the Vaiṣṇa-vas, it has two distinct recensions—the Bengal and the South-Indian. It is only the latter that is available in print.
Like some of the other पुराणस् this one also deals with a variety of subjects, only a few of which may be mentioned here: stories of ब्रह्मा’s sacrifice; legends connected with the sage दधीचि, Vṛtra, नहुष, ययाति, शकुन्तला and others; greatness of sacred rivers like गङ्गा and holy places like प्रयाग, काशी and गया; description of the various worlds of goblins, गन्धर्वस्, हेअवेन् and so on; varṇāśrama-dharmas; vratas or religious vows; śrāddhas of various types; ritualistic worship of विष्णु and शिव; importance of Sahasranāmas as those of विष्णु and राम; कर्म and its result.
It is obvious that it contains compositions of various persons written during various periods of time.
SKANDAPURĀṆA
Biggest of the extant पुराणस्, the Skandapurāṇa is found in two forms, one being divided into seven khaṇḍas and the other into six saṁhitās.
The seven khaṇḍas are: Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa, Brāhma-khaṇḍa, Kāśīkhaṇḍa, Āvantyakhaṇḍa, Nāgarakhaṇḍa and Prabhāsakhaṇḍa. There are 81,000 ślokas or verses spread over 1671 chapters.
The six saṁhitās are: Sanatkumāra-saṁhitā, सूतसṁहिता, Śaṅkarasaṁhitā, Vaiṣṇavasaṁhitā, Brāhmasaṁhitā and Saurasaṁhitā. The total number of verses in this series also comes to 81,000.
Of these, only the first three saṁhitās are available now in print, whereas all the seven khaṇḍas of the former have been printed.
This purāṇa is said to have been taught by शिव to पार्वती, पार्वती to स्कन्द (Ṣaṇmukha or कार्त्तिकेय or सुब्रह्मण्य), स्कन्द to नन्दि, नन्दि to अत्रि and अत्रि to व्यास.
The number of subjects dealt with in this work is legion. It contains numerous upākhyānas or stories, detailed descriptions of several places of पिल्ग्रिमगे of which काशी, पुरी and उज्जयिनी get the pride of place, Advaita Vedānta, various aspects of Lord शिव, his liṅgas and methods of meditation as also worship and varṇāśrama-dharmas. Another interesting feature is the geographical details it gives, of ancient India. The सत्यनारायण-व्रत which is very common and popular now, gets a prominent place in the Revākhaṇḍa part of the Āvantyakhaṇḍa.
This purāṇa has been the source of several minor works like Sahyādrikhaṇḍa, Kāśmīrakhaṇḍa, Ambikāmāhātmya, Arundhatīvratakathā and so on.
VĀMANAPURĀṆA
Said to have been taught by the sage पुलस्त्य to नारद, this purāṇa is primarily a Vaiṣṇava work. Though the ten avatāras of विष्णु, especially the Vāma-nāvatāra, get the pride of place, it has liberal views and deals with other deities also such as शिव, गणपति and सूर्य.
It is stated to consist of two parts, the second part being sometimes called Bṛhad-vāmanapurāṇa. Now, only the first part is available in print.
The birth and exploits of गणेश and कार्त्तिकेय, greatness of शिव, importance of the river गङ्गा, certain vratas or religious observances, doctrine of कर्म, legends of ब्रह्मा, प्रह्लाद, बलि and शुक्राचार्य, लिबेरतिओन् of Gajendra (the elephant king)—these are some of the topics dealt with in this work.
VARĀHAPURĀṆA
The printed text of the Varāhapurāṇa has only 10,000 verses as against the 24,000 mentioned in other पुराणस् like the Matsyapurāṇa. Perhaps this purāṇa was in two parts and only one of them has been recovered so far.
Lord विष्णु in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as Varāha (the Boar) is said to have given this teaching to भूदेवी (the Earth) at her request.
There are two recensions of this purāṇa: the Gauḍīya and the Dākṣiṇātya. They differ from each other in quite a few places.
This purāṇa deals with most of the general topics of the धर्मशास्त्रस् such as vratas, places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, दान (gifts), images of deities and their worship, अशौच (ceremonial impurity), śrāddha (after-death ceremonies), theory of कर्म, hells, चोस्मोलोग्य्, sins and their expiation and so on.
Two episodes of this purāṇa—the Madhurākhyāna and the Nāciketopā-khyāna—are well-known. The latter contains detailed descriptions of हेअवेन् and हेल्ल्.
VĀYUPURĀṆA
Whether the Vāyupurāṇa has to be listed among the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas or the Śivapurāṇa, has been a moot point. If some scholars opine that the two पुराणस् are one and the same called by different names, there are others who feel that the former is a part of the latter. However, all of them agree that the core content of this purāṇa is quite ancient.
It has four sections, designated as ‘pādas’, as follows: Prakriyāpāda, Anuṣaṅgapāda, Upodghātapāda and Upasaṁhārapāda.
This purāṇa is clearly a śaiva-पाशुपत work. Detailed geographical descriptions of places, of manvantaras (or the periods of मनु), the importance and the greatness of गया (the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे), genealogies of some kings and sages, several details of śrāddha ceremonies and the science of music—are some of the topics dealt with in this purāṇa.
VIṢṆUPURĀṆA
One of the oldest पुराणस्, the Viṣṇupurāṇa conforms fairly strictly to the characteristics generally ascribed to the पुराणस्. Detailed treatment of the vratas or tīrthas, which find a prominent place in the other पुराणस्, is conspicuous by its absence.
Spread over six sections—called aṁśas—and written in a mellifluous language, the work deals with the usual topics like च्रेअतिओन् of this world and of the deities and the manes, the stories of ध्रुव, प्रह्लाद, जडभरत, and Śrī राम, the वेदस्, the four varṇas and the four āśramas, the impact of कलि (personification of the Iron Age, and of irreligiosity) and so on. The story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—a precursor to the Bhāgavata—is given in detail.
Quite a few philosophical ideas of the वेदस् are reflected in this purāṇa. The description of the कलियुग, the age in which we are living now, seems to be astonishingly accurate. Though विष्णु has been given prominence, he is not one of the Trinity, but the origin of all the three, ब्रह्मन् Himself. भक्ति or devotion has been propagated as the main sādhana or means of attaining लिबेरतिओन्. On the whole, it is a highly readable purāṇa which has been quite popular and has attracted the attention of many scholars who have written commentaries on it.
Recurrent Topics of the Purāṇas
Though most of the पुराणस् are encyclopaedic in character, some subjects, like च्रेअतिओन् of this world, seem to recur frequently. These subjects may now be taken up for a brief exposition.
CREATION
Creation of this world is a topic that often engages the attention of the पुराणस्. The Vedāntic doctrine that ब्रह्मन्, the One without a second, is the ultimate Truth is accepted by all the पुराणस् though the sectarian deities like शिव or विष्णु, are sometimes identified with it. Evolution of the world takes place from प्रकृति or primeval matter (an aspect of ब्रह्मन्), the order of evolution being the same as expounded by the Sāṅkhya and the Vedānta philosophies: प्रकृति-महत्-अहङ्कार (ego sense), मनस् (mind), ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (organs of knowledge) and कर्मेन्द्रियस् (organs of action) as also the पञ्चभूतस् (the five primordial elements). These, the first evolutes, make up the ब्रह्माण्ड or the Cosmic Egg, also called हिरण्यगर्भ. ब्रह्मन् enters into it and causes further evolution right up to a blade of grass, the whole process being guided by the residual कर्म (or deserts) of the unredeemed jīvas (individual souls) carried over from the previous cycle of च्रेअतिओन्.
Different types and methods of च्रेअतिओन् are also given in some of the पुराणस्.
Creation is accepted to be cyclic (crea-tion-sustenance-destruction-recreation and so on), having no specific beginning or end.
Unlike the world that we see and know, this earth and the galaxies, the च्रेअतिओन् envisaged by the पुराणस् has fourteen lokas or worlds, seven subterranean and seven above. Unlike in the modern view, again, all the thirteen worlds different from ours, are inhabited by conscious living beings, acclimatised to the particular vibrations of those regions and endowed with suitable sensory receivers.
THE EARTH
The paurāṇic geography and astro-nomy are, to say the least, quite enigmatic to the modern मिन्द्. An account of this earth, as detailed in some पुराणस् like the Bhāgavata, depicts it as a circular body, with seven concentric circles or belts called dvīpas (continents) arranged one within the other, with oceans of different liquids surrounding each belt like moats. Each continent is described as having its own mountain and river-system. In the central continent called जम्बूद्वीप, stands Mahāmeru, the axis of the whole world systems. Along the fringe of the outermost continent runs the लोकालोक mountain. The single-wheeled chariot of सूर्य (the sun) circles along this mountain, creating day and night.
The whole description is evidently a schematic and symbolic representation for meditative purposes, to draw our attention from the gross to the subtle spirit pervading nature.
TIME
Another concept of the पुराणस् that boggles our मिन्द् is that of time as connected with च्रेअतिओन्.
Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Being, conducts the work of च्रेअतिओन् through ब्रह्मा the intermediary instrument. A cycle of च्रेअतिओन् is a day-time of ब्रह्मा and of dissolution, his night. This dissolution is ‘naimittika-प्रलय,’ quasi-dissolution only, of the worlds up to सत्यलोक. They manifest again during the day-time of ब्रह्मा. One year of ब्रह्मा consists of 360 such days and his life-span is 100 such years. The immensity of this is realised only if it is converted in terms of human years. One year of human beings is one day of the celestials. Twelve-thousand such celestial years form one catur-yuga (the period of four युगस् of Kṛta or सत्य, Tretā, Dvāpara and कलि). Two thousand such चतुर्युगस् constitute one day, including the night-time, of ब्रह्मा. The total duration of ब्रह्मा’s lifetime in terms of human years, comes to a little more than three lakh billion years!
Each day-time of ब्रह्मा (of one thousand चतुर्युगस्) is divided into fourteen Manvantaras or Epochs of मनुस् or Patriarchs. These Manus—like Svāyam-bhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttami and others—maintain the world-order and progress, under the directions of दिविने इन्चर्नतिओन्स्.
Every मन्वन्तर consists of about seventy-six चतुर्युगस्, each of which is marked by retrogression from the perfection of the Kṛta to the degradation of the कलि. The Lord will restore the balance at the end of the Caturyuga.
GENEALOGIES
The पुराणस् abound in long lists of genealogies of kings and sages. Since some names and their chronological order seem to be common, it may safely be assumed that these ancient personalities did exist. However, the details being scant, they do not enlighten us in any way to know our ancient history.
One of the traits found in these lists is the tendency to trace the different dynasties to a common ancestor, वैवस्वत मनु, son of सूर्य (sun). Four of his nine sons—Ikṣvāku, नाभानेदिष्ठ, Śaryāti and Nābhāga—were responsible for establishing four well-known dynasties: Aikṣvāku, Vaiśāla, Śāryāta and Rāthītara. They were all a part of the Sūryavaṁśa or the Solar dynasty. The चन्द्रवṁश or the lunar dynasty was founded by पुरूरवस् Aila.
Then, there are the genealogies of the sages, the सप्तर्षिस् (Seven Sages) and others, like गौतम, भरद्वाज, अत्रि, कश्यप and so on. These lists are also quite long.
As regards these genealogical lists, this much can be said that they point to the great antiquity of our civilization.
Purāṇas as Ancient Indian Historical Tradition
It is to be kept in मिन्द् that the paurāṇic concept of time is cyclic, based on the theory that च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and destruction (sṛṣṭi, sthiti and प्रलय) take place in a cyclic order, having no specific beginning or end. Since modern history is based on the linear concept of time, the historical traditions of the पुराणस् may appear to be enigmatic.
Events themselves pass away with their occurrence. However, they survive as memories registered in the psyche of the human beings and can stimulate them for creative activities. A chain of such powerful stimulations gets established as a tradition. The पुराणस् are repositories of such traditions from the most ancient times. Their utility lies in contributing to the continuity and betterment of the civilisation and culture of a people. Hence, though they may not fit into the frame-work of ‘history’ as defined by the modern man, they cannot be dismissed as fiction either! They were originally based on facts and hence can help us in reconstructing our history. For instance, the lists of the dynasties of kings, though they mention the originators of the dynasties like इक्ष्वाकु, also include the dynasties known to the historical period such as Śiśunāgas, Nandas, Mauryas, Guptas, and even the आभीरस्, यवनस् and Hūṇas.
Ethics of the Purāṇas
Dharma or duty constitutes the foundation of purāṇic एथिच्स्. It embraces all the factors which contribute to the progress and well-being of the individual, the society and the world at large. These factors include the possession of guṇas or virtues and कर्म or proper discharge of one’s duties.
The पुराणस् recognize two types of dharmas: sādhāraṇa or सामान्य धर्म (generic) and viśeṣa धर्म or स्वधर्म (specific).
The individual, being an integral part of the society owes a duty to himself and to the society. Since his rise and fall affect the society, he must endeavour to raise himself to the fullest stature.
Hence there is no conflict between the individual and the social duties.
Dharma contributes to the welfare and progress of the human society, nay, of the whole world. In the puruṣārtha scheme of life, धर्म occupies the first place. It is the best kith and kin of the embodied सोउल् not only in life, but also after death. It wanes from its full strength in the कृतयुग to only a quarter in the कलियुग.
The पुराणस् have successfully reconciled the sādhāraṇa-dharmas with स्वधर्म. Whereas the former comprise virtues that impart refinement and culture to an individual, the latter is a practical application of the former within a particular sphere by an individual belonging to a class characterised by certain prominent qualities or guṇas. The scheme of वर्ण and आश्रम dharmas which the पुराणस् unanimously advocate, is based upon the duties of the individuals of a class. It aims at material and spiritual perfection of the society as a whole.
The sādhāraṇa-dharmas are universal in scope and eternal in nature. Though the पुराणस् enumerate them generally as ten, a few more virtues are sometimes added, making the list longer. They are: अहिṁसा (non-injury), सत्य (truthfulness), kṣamā or kṣānti (forbearance), दम or इन्द्रियनिग्रह (self control), शम (inner peace), दया (compassion), दान (charity), शौच (purity), तपस् (austerity) and ज्ञान (wisdom).
Of these, सत्य and अहिṁसा are extolled highly. शौच (purity), both internal and external, is stressed as an indispensable socio-ethical virtue. तपस् which includes disinterested action is a must for achieving anything great in life. दान is also eulogised much as a social duty.
Coming to the viśeṣa-dharmas (svadharma) or varṇāśrama-dharmas, the पुराणस् deal with them extensively. The वर्ण system represents a natural division of the society based on गुण (nature) and कर्म (vocation). The आश्रम scheme of life helps an individual to evolve himself from the stage of a novice in pursuit of learning to the stage of a person ever living in God. Both these systems enjoin upon their individual members certain duties.
If a ब्राह्मण is advised to lead an austere life in pursuit of knowledge and spiritual excellence and give that know-ledge to others, a क्षत्त्रिय is exhorted to protect the society from external aggression and help maintain internal law and order. A वैश्य is to engage himself in the production and distribution of wealth and goods through agriculture, dairy farming and trade. Those incapable of pursuing these three modes of life lived by serving the others and became the शूद्रस्.
Coming to the āśramas or the four stages of life, ब्रह्मचर्य or studenthood comes first. It is the period of study and discipline spent in the होउसे of the गुरु. Service to the गुरु is an essential aspect of this life.
Gārhasthya or householdership is the next stage of life. Since it offers the largest scope for service and sacrifice, it is considered as the most vital stage. The householder is the refuge and main stay for those in the other three stages of life. Earning his livelihood by right means and performing the पञ्चयज्ञस् (five daily sacrifices like worship of the gods, study of the वेदस् and feeding living beings) form an integral part of his life.
The वानप्रस्थ (life of a forest-recluse) is the third stage and is only a preparation for the final stage of renunciation. Simple life and contemplation on God are its essential features.
Saṁnyāsa (life of a monk) is the last stage where the saṁnyāsin (monk) has to live a life of total detachment from the world, depending solely on God and ever meditating on him.
Other ideas that find a place in the पुराणस् are the theory of कर्म and पुनर्जन्म (transmigration), prāyaścittas (expiations for sins), vratas (religious observances) and तीर्थयात्रा (pilgrimage).
‘As you sow, so you reap’ is the principle behind the theory of कर्म. Since actions always produce their corresponding results, human beings are advised to eschew evil and always do good. Effect of sins committed, knowingly or unknowingly, can be got rid of, or at least minimised, by performing proper expiations prescribed for them.
Vratas or religious observances with their stress on ड़स्तिन्ग् and self-control help in self-purification. So also तीर्थयात्रा or visiting places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, associated with gods or saints.
Popular Religion in the Purāṇas
The labyrinth of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् on one side and the uncompromising way of renunciation as taught by the Upaniṣadic sages on the other, both of which were beyond the reach of the common masses, drove the ordinary people, whose hunger for religion was no less sincere, into the arms of बुद्धिस्म् and जैनिस्म्. It was at this juncture that the पुराणस् as we know them today, started evolving. The paths of कर्म and भक्ति, with their various ramifications were gradually introduced into them. Over the centuries they have grown both in quantity and in quality, so much so, that they are now the bed-rock of modern हिन्दुइस्म्.
Temples and temple rituals, domestic worship along with the associated religious rites, vratas (religious vows and festivals) and तीर्थयात्रा (pilgrimage) invariably find a prominent place in the पुराणस्. Sometimes, details of construction of temples and their consecration are also given.
Instructions regarding ritualistic worship, both independently and as a part of the vratas, also find a place. They include aspects of austerity associated with them such as ड़स्तिन्ग् and keeping vigil.
Of the sixteen सṁस्कारस् or sacraments, only śrāddha (obsequial rites) has been given a pre-eminent place though the others also are dealt with.
Bhakti or devotion to God (especially towards the well-known deities of the Hindu pantheon, including the avatāras or incarnations) is another subject dealt with in great detail in the पुराणस्. They extol the extraordinary powers of the mantras (divine names) and have also given substantial information about the science of the mantras (mantraśāstra). However, the general trend is always towards stressing the unity of the Godhead and emphasising that the various deities are only its aspects. Vilification of some deities and their followers is an exception and may safely be brushed aside as an aberration or as interpolations by fanatics.
Upapurāṇas
Though tradition fixed the number of the Mahāpurāṇas as eighteen, the growth of purāṇa literature went on unabated. Hence those of the पुराणस् which did not or could not find a place in that list were accommodated under the title ‘Upapurāṇas’. In course of time the number of these उपपुराणस् also got fixed at eighteen. They were considered as appendices to the Mahāpurāṇas and hence of lesser importance. However, quite a few of them are large enough in size and important enough in content, that they compel us to treat them with respect. The number also has exceeded eighteen.
The lists of these उपपुराणस्, as given in the various Mahāpurāṇas do not tally. Some of the पुराणस् listed under the Mahāpurāṇas, as for instance, Brahmāṇda or Vāmana, find a place in the lists of उपपुराणस् also. Some of these उपपुराणस् are: Ādi, Nārasiṁha, Kāpila, Kālikā, Vāruṇa, Bṛhannandi, Ekāmra, Viṣṇudharmottara and Devī-bhāgavata.
According to some writers, the Devībhāgavata is the real Bhāgavata and not the Śrīmad Bhāgavata (or Viṣṇu-bhāgavata) which is only an Upapurāṇa.
The general content of these उपपुराणस् is identical with those of the Mahāpurāṇas. However, they are more sectarian in character interested in propagating their own cults.
Conclusion
From this brief survey of the पुराणस् it can safely be conceded that they have admirably succeeded in preserving and propagating Hindu religion and culture, especially through the critical periods of our history. Their simple exposition of the Vedāntic principles of philosophy, explanation of the various aspects of धर्म (conduct and duties) and inducing people to follow धर्म in their life, stress on the performance of स्वधर्म, exhortations as to दान (gifts) and sevā (service) to mankind to maintain social balance, advice to keep up religious harmony, their providing simple and popular modes of worship, especially to women and the backward classes, have contributed immensely to the growth and the sustenance of the Hindu ethos. A lot of historical facts, though mixed up with myths, contained in them can help us to reconstruct Indian history, freeing it from the distortions and prejudices of the European writers and Anglicised Indians.
They therefore deserve a far more careful study than has hitherto been devoted to them.

Purandaradāsa
(A. D. 1484-1564)
------------------------------------------
The Haridāsas of Karnataka have contributed significantly to the भक्ति Movement, the religious movement that chiefly propagated the cult of भक्ति or devotion to God, as the best means of spiritual evolution.
Purandaradāsa was a pioneer in this field.
His biographical details as have come down to us by oral traditions seem to be more mythical than real or historical. Piecing together all such details as are available now, his life can briefly be stated as follows:
PurandaradāsaHe was born sometime in A. D. 1484. His ड़थेर्, Varadappa Nāyaka, who was a fabulously rich diamond merchant, christened him as Śrīnivasa Nāyaka and educated him not only in the traditional learning—Sanskrit and scriptures—but also in मुसिच् and the family occupation.
In course of time he became a fine young man and was married to a pious girl सरस्वती from a decent family. He then took over his ड़थेर्’s business and further improved upon it.
In spite of immense wealth he was a miser to the core. He never helped the people who were in distress and approached him for assistance. Once a miraculous incident, for which his pious wife was the cause, totally transformed his life. He distributed all his wealth to the needy, became a beggar for the sake of God and approached the great sage व्यासतीर्थ (A. D. 1447-1539) for initiation into spiritual life. The sage readily obliged and gave him the new name Purandara-dāsa.
Since then, पुरन्दरदास spent the rest of his life, until his final departure from this world (in A. D. 1564), in spiritual pursuits, spreading the cult of devotion to God and the message of moral regeneration among the people, both the classes and the masses.
Kanakadāsa (A. D. 1508-1606), another great saint, was his contemporary.
The most valuable contribution of पुरन्दरदास is in the field of classical and devotional मुसिच्, now well-known as South Indian or Carnatic मुसिच्. He greatly simplified the methods of teaching, as also learning, which are being followed even today.
Almost all his songs are in Kannada, the lingua franca of the Karnataka State and the rest in Sanskrit. Though he is said to have composed 4,25,000 songs, only about a thousand are available now. Even among these, it is difficult to say which ones are his original or real compositions.
Since he toured the country extensively, visiting most of the important places of Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे, the maximum number of his compositions are devoted to a nice description of these places.
Other topics dealt with in them are: the philosophy of मध्वाचार्य (A. D. 1238-1317) to which school or cult he belonged; the great teachers of this school; various celestial worlds; stories and anecdotes from the पुराणस्; descriptions of gods and goddesses; daily routine of a devotee of God, especially a ब्राह्मण; and devotional songs on the various aspects of God.
He is also reputed to have authored some independent literary works like the Draupadīvastrāpaharaṇa, Sudāmacaritra and Paratattvasāra. However, none of these is available now.
See also DĀSAKŪṬA.

Puruṣottama
(‘the best of human beings’)
------------------------------------------
The literal meaning of the word is ‘the best of men.’ However, it is often used to indicate God, especially in his aspect as Lord विष्णु.
After dividing this world into two classes of puruṣas—the kṣarapuruṣas (bound souls) and the akṣarapuruṣas (the liberated ones)—the Bhagavadgītā (16.16-18) declares that God (= Śrī कृष्ण here) is पुरुषोत्तम, the best of beings, who has transcended the other two.
The well-known Viṣṇusahasranāma (24) uses this word also to indicate the Lord विष्णु. Out of the several interpretations a few may be given here:
He is the best of men.
It is ब्रह्मन् who is called पुरुषोत्तम.
It is he who is complete and perfect.
He is superior even to the creator ब्रह्मा.
It is he who makes human beings superior to animals and the subhuman species.

Purāṇasāra
------------------------------------------
This is a voluminous work of 6000 verses spread over 84 adhyāyas or chapters. विद्यारण्य (A. D. 1296-1386) is said to be the author. Since the colophon at the end states the name of the author as माधवाचार्य, son of Māyaṇa, the work must have been composed before his सṁन्यास.
It is actually a compilation of all the important topics contained in the 18 पुराणस्. Other works included in its purview are: Rāmāyaṇa, महाभारत, मनुस्मृति, Yājñavalkyasmṛti, पराशर-mādhavīya, Jaiminīya-āśvamedhikaparva, Puruṣārthasudhānidhi, हरिवṁश and Viṣṇucitti-ātmaprakāśa.
The ślokas are often reproduced from the originals as they are.
The following is a list of the subjects dealt with in this work:
Characteristics of the पुराणस् and the उपपुराणस्; Advaita Vedānta; the One as the many; च्रेअतिओन्; on the वेदस् and प्रणव; the four varṇas and the various jātis that are the offshoots of mixing; युगस् and manvantaras; speciality of the कलियुग; duties of a king; उपनयन and the duties of a ब्रह्मचारिन्; duties of a गृहस्थ, वानप्रस्थ and a यति; sadā-cāra or good conduct; śrāddha ceremony; prāyaścittas or expiations; यवनस् and दस्युस् (non-Āryan tribes); सामान्य- dharmas (dharmas common to all); on gurubhakti (devotion to the गुरु); devotion towards and service to the parents; devotion to God in all his aspects such as शिव, विष्णु and देवी; authority of the Śāstras; duties of women; various continents of the earth; various lokas or worlds; development of the child in the womb; Viṣṇumāyā; sufferings in यमलोक or the world of यम; svargaloka or हेअवेन् is ephemeral; rebirth depends on सṁस्कारस् or past tendencies; desire-motivated actions decried; aṣṭāṅgayoga described; various āsanas; four kinds of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्; the four पुरुषार्थस्; greatness of Śivamantra; on ariṣṭas or prognostication and how to overcome them; on ब्रह्मज्ञान; विश्वरूप of शिव; number of ślokas and phalaśruti.
The work gives several stories culled from the various पुराणस्. Some have been quoted in full whereas the others have been given in an abridged form.
The following is a list of such stories that appear in this work: ब्रह्मा and विष्णु trying to find out the extent of the शिवलिङ्ग; अरुन्धती’s devoted service to her husband वसिष्ठ; Jājalī taught by तुलाधार; story of Śambūka and his death at the hands of राम; sacrifice of emperor शिबि to save a pigeon; king नहुष’s arrogance; stories of sages like आरुणि, Yavakrīta and अणिमाण्डव्य; sage Saubhari falling from the ideal; sage Mandapāla’s लिबेरतिओन्; story of the king Ila who alternately became a man and a woman due to a curse; story of the king कार्तवीर्यार्जुन who was ultimately killed by परशुराम; Puṇḍarīka, the devotee of Viṭṭhala; स्वयṁवर of द्रौपदी; stories of परशुराम, Śantanu and अम्बा; king Śveta who was a राजर्षि and a devotee of Lord Jagannātha; king सुरथ, the devotee of the Divine मोथेर्; birth of कुमार or स्कन्द to शिव and पार्वती; story of the child-devotee प्रह्लाद; Śīlavatī, the पतिव्रता (devoted wife) who continued to serve her immoral husband; धर्मव्याध, the devoted son; loss and regaining of the jewel स्यमन्तकमणि; ययाति’s insatiable lust; king इन्द्रद्युम्न and अगस्त्य’s curse; जडभरत the great अवधूत (perfected सोउल्); Asita देवल, the great sage.
Since the Purāṇasāra is only a compendium wherein much of the material has been taken verbatim from the source books, not much can be said about its originality.
However, it serves very well as a ready-reckoner for a knowledge of the पुराणस्.
See also PURĀṆAS and VIDYĀRAṆYA.

pūrṇakumbha
(‘pot filled [with water]’)
------------------------------------------
A पूर्णकुम्भ is a sacred symbol of prosperity. Other names for the same are: pūrṇaghaṭa and pūrṇakalaśa.
It is a part and parcel of many rituals since it indicates auspiciousness.
It is prepared by filling up a pot of silver or copper with water, to which may be added certain scents, and the mouth covered with mango leaves and a coconut.
When an important guest or an invitee for a sacred function arrives, he is to be received with पूर्णकुम्भ accompanied by the chanting of Vedic mantras that generally include the शान्तिमन्त्रस् and selected portions from the उपनिषद्स्.
Sculptural representations of pūrṇa-kumbha are frequently seen in temples from very early times. They are shown on walls and pillars in a variety of decorative arrangements.

Puraścaryārṇava
------------------------------------------
This is an encyclopaedic work on the mantraśāstra or the science of mantras. The title of the work actually means that it is an ocean (‘arṇava’) of mantras, the proper repetition of which leads to the particular deity presenting itself before (‘puraś-चरण’ or ‘puraś-चर्या’) the sādhaka or the votary.
The king Pratāpasiṁha Ṣā of Nepal (rule A. D. 1774-1777) is the author of this voluminous work. He is credited to have organised a conference of Sanskrit scholars from twelve countries.
This treatise has twelve taraṅgas or chapters dealing with various aspects of the main subject. The following table gives an idea of its contents:
First Taraṅga — Details of the various चक्रस्.
Second Taraṅga — Offering through germinated seeds.
Third Taraṅga — Selecting the गुरु and worship of the deity.
Fourth Taraṅga — Mode of Kriyāvatīdīkṣā.
Fifth Taraṅga — Various kinds of दीक्षा.
Sixth Taraṅga — On पुरश्चरण in general.
Seventh Taraṅga — Different kinds of पुरश्चरण and the fulfilment of their mantras.
Eighth Taraṅga — Mantras of गणपति and other deities like नरसिṁह.
Ninth Taraṅga — Puraścaraṇa of the mantras of दशमहाविद्यास्.
Tenth Taraṅga — Puraścaraṇa of Vedic mantras like गायत्री.
Eleventh Taraṅga — Puraścaraṇa of दुर्गा मन्त्र and mode of observing दुर्गोत्सव.
Twelfth Taraṅga — Puraścaraṇa of the मन्त्र of ब्राह्मी and others as also about yantras.

The various subjects dealt with in this work may now be dealt with briefly under different headings.
Puraścaraṇa
Puraścaraṇa is actually a special religious rite consisting of five steps. They are: जप (repetition of the मन्त्र received from the गुरु); होम (ritual oblations into a duly consecrated fire); तर्पण (satiating the deity through offering water or milk); मार्जन (sprinkling water on one’s own head with the मन्त्र of the deity); ब्राह्मण भोजन (feeding the ब्राह्मणस्).
The whole process is centred round the primary requisite called दीक्षा, ceremonially receiving the मन्त्र (sacred formula or word) from a qualified गुरु.
The Guru
Only a person of purity with a fund of knowledge of all aspects of the subject and endowed with the competence necessary to give दीक्षा can become a गुरु.
The following are some of the traits he is expected to possess: a pleasant appearance; expert knowledge of the आगमस् and the methods of giving mantras; introversion; power of grace and admonition; compassion towards all beings; self-control; contentment; love of disciples; impartiality; engaging in pure and prescribed activities; respect towards women; equanimity; freedom from the अरिषड्वर्ग or six evils like lust and anger; detachment towards women and wealth.
The Disciple
If the गुरु has to be well-qualified to give दीक्षा, the शिष्य or the disciple too must possess basic traits of character conducive to sādhanā or spiritual practice.
Some of these have been listed as follows: desire for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्; faith in and great respect towards the गुरु; a certain degree of self-control and purity of मिन्द्; devotion to truth; alert intelligence, capable of grasping the गुरु’s teaching quickly; control over speech; devoted service to the गुरु; humility; dexterity in action.
Dīkṣā
When a मन्त्र is given by the गुरु (‘dīyate’) the sins of the disciple are destroyed (‘kṣīyate’). Hence the process is called दीक्षा.
Dīkṣā is of four kinds: Kriyāvatī, Varṇamayī, Kalāvatī and Vedhamayī (See under TANTRAS.).
Sometimes three more are added. They are: sparśadīkṣā, vāgdīkṣā and dṛgdīkṣā (See under TANTRAS.).
Though दीक्षा can be taken at all times, the three seasons—vasanta (spring), śarad (autumn) and śiśira (winter)—are recommended as better. And, सूर्य- ग्रहण or the time of solar एच्लिप्से has been especially favoured as extremely auspicious.
As regards the spots suitable for दीक्षा, the work mentions 16 places. Out of these, a pilgrim centre and a शिव temple are considered as best.
It is interesting to note that different places have been favoured as suitable for the जप of different mantras, as follows:
Bank of नर्मदा river for Gaṇeśamantra; प्रभास and कुरुक्षेत्र for Sūryamantra; गया and द्वारका for Viṣṇumantra; bank of गङ्गा river and रामेश्वरम् for शिव मन्त्र; ज्वालामुखी and प्रयाग for शक्ति or देवी मन्त्र.
However, dilapidated places as also crowded places must be totally avoided.
As per this and other traditional treatises, the दीक्षा has to be given in a specially erected मण्डप or shed built strictly according to stipulated norms.
Mantras and Cakras
Mantra is that syllable or word or words by reflecting upon which, one can get all knowledge and is protected against the bondage of सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
A मन्त्र and the deity it represents are identical.
About 54 mantras pertaining to various deities (including several aspects of the same deity) have been given in this work.
Some of these deities are: अन्नपूर्णा; Bālā; चामुण्डा; दक्षिणामूर्ति; दुर्गा; एकजटा; गणेश; गौरी; हनुमान्; हयग्रीव; Kālī; Kārttavīryārjuna; कृष्ण; कुबेर; महालक्ष्मी; Mṛtyuñjaya; Nṛsiṁha; परशुराम; राम; शनि; सरस्वती; सीता; शीतला; सूर्य; Tvaritā; उच्छिष्ट-गणपति; वामन; वनदुर्गा; यम.
When a would-be disciple approaches a गुरु for mantradīkṣā, it is the responsi-bility of the गुरु to find out a मन्त्र that suits him. This can be done by consulting an appropriate चक्र or table. The treatise has mentioned eleven चक्रस् with the associated details. They are Ahibalacakra; Akaḍamacakra; Akathahacakra; Kulākulacakra; Kūrmacakra; Nakṣatracakra; Rāśicakra; Ṛṇidhanicakra; Ṣaṭpadamātṛkācakra; Uditacakra; Vargacakra.
Except the Kūrmacakra, all the others are used in determining the suitabi- lity of a मन्त्र for the disciple. Generally the first letter of the name of the disciple and the first letter of the proposed मन्त्र are checked through these चक्रस् to know whether it is suitable for him.
In the case of the Nakṣatracakra, the suitability of a मन्त्र is determined by referring to the birth नक्षत्र of the disciple and the नक्षत्र of the first letter of the मन्त्र as given in the table.
As regards the Rāśicakra, similar calculation is done based on the राशि of birth of the disciple and the राशि of the first letter of the मन्त्र as found in the table.
Niyamas or Rules
A disciple who wants to undertake पुरश्चरण has to regulate his life by following some basic rules: Getting up at the brāhmīmuhūrta (about one hour before sunrise), finishing ablutions and bath, completing the usual daily rituals like सन्ध्या and पूजा. The disciple can then start his पुरश्चरण.
Other rules mentioned are: sleeping on the कुश-mat spread on the ground; observing ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and mauna (silence); taking sāttvik ड़ोओद् like milk, fruits and vegetables; serving the गुरु; performing special pūjās when prescribed; chanting of hymns and singing devotional songs.
He has to completely avoid taking ड़ोओद् in others’ houses, the ariṣaḍvargas (the six enemies of spiritual life like lust and anger), evil speech and falsehood, profane मुसिच् and decorating one’s person.
Once he fixes the number of the जप (as for instance, 100 mālās per day), he should strictly keep it up, doing neither more nor less.
It has been suggested that he should have ड़ोओद् only once and that too, at night.
If any of these rules are broken the prāyaścittas (expiations) prescribed for them like the जप of the गायत्री, should be performed.
Āsanas or Seats
The āsanas or seats normally recommended to be used during the पुरश्चरण rites should be made of any of the following materials; कुश grass (Poa cynosuroides); अजिन (deer-skin); ambara (soft cotton) and kambala (wool).
As regards the woollen seats, different coloured ones are prescribed for different results such as white one for धर्म (virtue) or red one for अर्थ (gaining wealth).
If the पुरश्चरण is being done for the fulfilment of any particular desire—by repeating the appropriate mantra—then different kinds of seats are prescribed as follows:
For attaining all desires — Tiger-skin
For relief from diseases — Sheep-skin
For nourishment — Silk
For attaining wealth — Cane

Seats used in sorcerous rites should be of various colours, as for instance, black for harming, red for controlling, others.
A seat made of buffalo skin is recommended for māraṇa (killing) rites.
The following materials should never be used in manufacturing the seats: wood, grass, stone and clay. They will produce harmful effects.
Āsanas or Postures
The following āsanas or yogic postures are recommended for जप of the मन्त्र, during पुरश्चरण: Kūrmāsana; पद्मासन; Siddhāsana; Svastikāsana; वीरासन.
Japamālās or Rosaries
A जपमाला is used for keeping the count during जप.
The mālās are made of various materials such as रुद्राक्ष (Elaeocarpus ganitrus), मणि (precious stones such as coral or pearl), शङ्ख (conch), sphaṭika (crystal), padmabīja (lotus-seeds) and dried sticks of तुलसी (holy basil).
Sometimes other materials like कुश grass (Poa cynosuroides), beads of gold or iron or copper and lākṣā (lac) are also used, mostly for desire-motivated rites.
Of all the mālās, रुद्राक्ष mālās are considered as the best and therefore most widely used.
A रुद्राक्ष bead may have 1 to 14 mukhas or faces, each one giving a different result.
The mālās are generally prepared by stringing with thread. Cotton thread has to be used for Vaiṣṇavīmālās (mālās used by Vaiṣṇavas to count विष्णु mantras). For Śaivīmālās (used by Śaivas and Śāktas to count शिव’s or देवी’s mantras) woollen thread or bark-thread is preferred.
The thread should be threefold and should have no knots.
A new mālā should first be washed in पञ्चगव्य (See PAÑCAGAVYA.) and then worshipped with certain Vedic mantras.
Counting of the mantras can be done by using the fingers of the hand, i.e., by using the spaces between the joints in the fingers. This is given the name, ‘karamālā’.
Some Related Topics
Quite a few topics have been discussed in this work which are related to the main subject of पुरश्चरण. They may now be described briefly.
If a disciple is unable to take bath before दीक्षा due to health reasons or other factors like old age ailments or even vagaries of weather he is given मन्त्र-स्नान or dhyānasnāna.
Mantrasnāna consists of sprinkling water on one’s feet, आचमन (See ĀCAMANA.), and some simple nyāsas (See under TANTRAS.).
Dhyānasnāna is done by meditating on विष्णु and imagining that the water springing from his feet is falling on one’s head, entering into the body through the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (aperture on the top of the head) and thus purifying the whole body.
As regards giving the मन्त्र by the गुरु, he has to keep his right hand on the head of the disciple and utter the मन्त्र in his right ear thrice.
Though mantras can be given to women and शूद्रस् also, only those mantras ending in ‘namaḥ’ should be given and not others.
If, by chance, a मन्त्र is received in dream, if that मन्त्र is in accordance with the scriptural injunctions, it can be taken, after writing it in vermillion on a banyan leaf and placing it before a कलश (pot of water) in which one’s गुरु is invoked.
Japa or Repetition of the Divine name
Since the whole rite of पुरश्चरण is centred round जप, some details regarding the same have to be given.
Japa can be practised at all times. However पुरश्चरण has to be started on the aṣṭamī (eighth day) or the caturdaśī (fourteenth day) of both the fortnights.
As regards the number it can be: 1008; 554; 300; 108.
The मन्त्र should be repeated neither fast nor slowly, but at medium speed.
Though there are three ways of doing japa—vācika (loudly), upāṁśu (in whispering tone) and mānasa (mentally)—mānasajapa is recommended as the best.
Before using the जपमाला, it has to be propitiated with certain mantras.
While using it for जप, use it with the right hand held near the heart, only the middle finger for supporting it should be used keeping the index finger away. The beads have to be pulled downwards with the thumb, one at a time, simultaneous with the repetition of the मन्त्र. The मेरु (the centrally fixed extra bead) should never be crossed.
For all kāmya rites, जपमाला must be used.
At the end of each session of जप, its result has to be offered at the feet of the deity of the मन्त्र, in the prescribed manner.
Kūrmacakra
Once the sādhaka who has taken mantradīkṣā or initiation in a मन्त्र, from a qualified गुरु, decides to do पुरश्चरण, especially for a particular purpose, he should choose a good place for its performance. This can be anywhere, in a city, in a village or even in one’s own होउसे.
On the spot thus selected, the Kūrmacakra has to be inscribed. First, a square has to be drawn with nine squares inside it. Then the drawing of a कूर्म or tortoise has to be inscribed in it, with the head towards the east and tail towards the west. Various letters of the Sanskrit alphabet have to be written inside it in the prescribed manner.
The sādhaka is advised to sit in the place of the mukha (head or face) for जप to get the maximum results. Sitting in other places of the चक्र gives inferior results, the worst being the tail portion.
However, in sacred places of pil-grimage, the Kūrmacakra is not necessary.
Havana or Homa
After जप, हवन or होम has to be done. The number of offerings is 1/10 of the number of जप. For instance, if the जप done for that day is 10,000, the होम-offerings should be 1000.
The fire for the होम can be brought from the होउसे of a ब्राह्मण. Alternatively, it can also be generated by striking flint stones or by araṇīs (See ARAṆI for details.).
The मन्त्र for the offering is the same as the mūlamantra (original मन्त्र) used in जप. However, the format is adjusted suitably for होम. It the mūlamantra is ‘Rāma’, the मन्त्र for हवन will be ‘Oṁ Rāmāya स्वाहा’.
The fire can be placed in a kuṇḍa (pit) or a small platform or even on the ground.
The work prohibits women and शूद्रस् from performing होम. Instead, they have to do more जप.
Tarpaṇa or Satiation
Tarpaṇa is done by offering milk or water to the deity using the same मन्त्र as for हवन.
The number should be 1/10 of the number of offerings in होम. In the example quoted above, it should be 100.
This milk or water is expected to be consumed by the performer-sādhaka.
Mārjana or Wiping
Using the mūlamantra with ‘namaḥ’ (for e.g., ‘Rāmāya namaḥ’) water has to be sprinkled on one’s own head with kumbhamudrā. The number of such mārjanas is 1/10 that of तर्पण. In the example given, it comes to 10.
Brāhmaṇabhojana
Brāhmaṇabhojana or feeding the ब्राह्मणस् is the last item of पुरश्चरण.
The number of ब्राह्मणस् to be invited is 1/10 that of मार्जन. In the example given above, it comes to one.
The ब्राह्मणस् should be invited with great respect and taken care of properly. They should be fed well with ṣaḍrasa-भोजन or ड़ोओद् of six kinds. Proper दक्षिणा (gifts) should also be offered.
This last rite is said to be so powerful that it can offset all the defects that might have crept in, during the performance of पुरश्चरण.
After the पुरश्चरण is completed, the गुरु has to be suitably honoured with ड़ोओद्, clothes and other presents.
Conclusion
If due to any reason, हवन and other rites cannot be performed, the treatise prescribes extra जप to compensate for the same.
It is thus seen that the work covers all important aspects of पुरश्चरण and can be a good handbook to all the sādhakas of mantrajapa.
It has paid particular attention to the chanting and all the associated rituals of the Saptaśatī or Durgāsaptaśatī at the end, since that work is considered as a basic scripture of mantraśāstra, the seince of mantras.

puruṣārthas
(‘ends [to be striven for by] human beings’)
------------------------------------------
Recognising the basic needs and cravings of a human being, the ancient sages of हिन्दुइस्म् have given a fourfold ideal to be striven for, by everyone. This is called the पुरुषार्थस् or the ends to be striven for in life.
They are four: धर्म (righteousness), अर्थ (wealth), काम (desires of the flesh) and मोक्ष (liberation from transmigratory existence).
Ordinary enjoyments of the world are centred round अर्थ and काम. However, in this world of cut-throat competition, unless some higher norms and standards—the right rules for a good and a fair game—are set up, the big fish will eat up the smaller ones and the jungle-law will prevail.
It is these rules that are indicated by the omnibus term धर्म.
Every person is free to pursue the path of अर्थ and काम, comfort and pleasure, but always within the perimeters of धर्म.
However, life teaches everyone, at least the more cultured and refined ones, that neither अर्थ nor काम can ever be satiated; and, that there must be a much higher goal to be sought after. This is मोक्ष or total लिबेरतिओन् from the transmigratory cycle of birth and death, and, being reinstated in one’s original state, the state of eternal bliss.
This can be attained through spiritual evolution under the guidance of expert spiritual masters.
Sometimes, the first three are grouped as one unit called ‘trivarga’ and the last as ‘apavarga’ (‘that which is beyond the three’).
As applied to a king, the four पुरुषार्थस् recommended are: desire for wealth that he does not have; protecting the wealth that he already has; developing and increasing that wealth; and, using it according to धर्म (vide Manusmṛti 7.99).
Here, the word ‘artha’ (in ‘puru-śārtha’) is taken only as ‘wealth’.

Purāṇasaṁhitā
(‘collection of ancient anecdotes’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् are extremely popular in the Hindu society even today. Many of the religious rites and practices as also temple rituals are based on, or, connected with, the पुराणस्.
The basic material of these पुराणस् lies in the gāthās (metrical songs or proverbial sayings), ākhyāyikās (ancient tales), upākhyānas (anecdotes) and kalpoktis (old sayings), often referred to even in the Vedic literature.
The sage व्यास is said to have compiled them all into one treatise called the Purāṇasaṁhitā, which became the basic work for the later पुराणस् and उपपुराणस्.
See PURĀṆAS also.

Pūrṇaprajña
(‘one whose spiritual wisdom is complete or perfect’)
------------------------------------------
See MADHVĀCĀRYA.

pūrṇapātra
(‘a vessel which is full’)
------------------------------------------
In वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् like Darśapūrṇa-māsa, it refers to a vessel, full of water, from which the priest अध्वर्यु pours water into the joined hands of the wife (of the yajamāna or the sacrificer) who is holding the योक्त्र (cord of muñja grass used as a belt) in them. A मन्त्र from the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (1.1.10.2) has to be chanted at that time.
At the end of a होम performed as per the तन्त्रस् (Śāktāgamas) a पूर्णपात्र has to be gifted. This is called ‘pūrṇa-pātradāna’. It consists of keeping in a plate all the ingredients needed for a full meal—like uncooked rice, gram, ghee, oil, salt, fruits and sweets along with a coin as दक्षिणा or cash-gift—and give it to a ब्राह्मण after the होम.
As a substitute for such a पूर्णपात्र, one can offer a vessel of sufficient quantity of rice (enough for a single meal), some fruits and a coin.
Before giving it away, it has to be sanctified with appropriate mantras.

puruṣa
(‘[one who] sleeps in the city [of nine gates or the body]’)
------------------------------------------
In common usage, the word ‘puruṣa’ means a man.
A good man should have these five qualities: giving gifts to deserving persons; appreciating the good in others; feeling happy in the company of relatives and friends; erudition in the scriptures; capacity to fight for a righteous cause.
He should also have great self-control.
In the उपनिषद्स् the word has often been used to indicate the जीव (the Self) as also the परमात्मन् (the Supreme सोउल् or God).
The Sāṅkhya philosophy uses it as a technical term indicating the individual सोउल्. In Sanskrit grammar it is used to denote the first, the second and the third persons.

purohita
(‘one who is engaged in rites that give their fruits here and hereafter’)
------------------------------------------
Right from the most ancient days, the Hindu sages had recognised the need for a king or a ruler to protect and control the society. Similarly they had also recognised the need for the king to be guided by a पुरोहित (chaplain of the State), not only in matters of religion but also in other fields like the dispensing of justice. Their philosophy behind statecraft was that only a balanced combination of the kingly and the priestly powers could guarantee the complete well-being of the State.
A king was to select a पुरोहित endowed with the following qualities: He should be a ब्राह्मण from a good family, possessing great learning, eloquence and pure character. He must be a handsome person of middle age. He should also be well-versed in the science of portents, and, the rites to be performed to offset the evil effects indicated by the portents.
His position was often hereditary; hence the term ‘kulapurohita’.
(Incidentally, even the देवस् or the gods and the असुरस् or the demons are said to have had kulapurohitas! The names of बृहस्पति and शुक्राचार्य are often mentioned in the वेदस् and the पुराणस् as the two kulapurohitas of these two races.)
His status was considered as even superior to that of the mantrins or the ministers.
If and when a king wanted to perform a Vedic sacrifice, the advice of the पुरोहित was of supreme importance in selecting the ṛtivks (priests).
Even in the modern days, the Hindu society very much depends on the पुरोहित or the priest for the performance of religious rites whether at home or in temples or in public/social functions. Some of these rites are: performance of the सṁस्कारस् (sacraments) like उपनयन (thread-ceremony) विवाह (marriage) and śrāddha (obsequial ceremonies); all ceremonies connected with the temple worship; religious rites like होम performed for the good of the society.
Though these ceremonies include Vedic mantras, they are based more on the आगमस् and पुराणस्.

pūrṇāhuti
(‘[the final] offering which completes [the sacrifice]’)
------------------------------------------
In वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् the word means offering a ladle-full of ghee into the fire. The final offering is made by the priest, in the standing posture. This is then followed by the yajamāna or sacrificer giving gifts to the priests.
In many other homas, performed according to the आगमस् and the तन्त्रस्, पूर्णाहुति represents the final offering (with appropriate mantras) indicating the completion of the rite. In such āhutis, the materials used are cloth, coconut, flowers, ताम्बूल (arecanuts and betel leaves), all of them being soaked in ghee.
